insidious

in-SID-ee-us -- stress on the second syllable, SID. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Insidious is treacherous and subtly harmful; spreading damage gradually and stealthily.

The illness was insidious, quietly sapping her strength for months before the first clear symptom appeared.

Example

A streaming app's autoplay feature is insidious: it starts the next episode before the credits finish, and a student who sat down for one twenty-minute show looks up to find the whole evening gone -- again.

The harm arrives so gradually and quietly that you never notice the moment it takes hold. Insidious dangers -- diseases, habits, influences -- do their damage before anyone thinks to look for them.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

stealthy: Stealthy describes the quiet, careful way something moves to avoid notice -- a stealthy cat, a stealthy approach. Insidious adds what the quietness is for: damage, spreading bit by bit while it goes unseen. A stealthy scout may be harmless; an insidious disease is doing harm the whole time.

sneaky: Sneaky is the everyday, small-scale word for dodging notice, usually in minor mischief -- a sneaky peek at the answers, a sneaky shortcut. Insidious is far graver: something hidden doing real damage the whole time it goes unseen. A sneaky trick embarrasses someone; an insidious influence quietly ruins something.

lurking: A lurking danger is present and hidden but has not struck yet -- the shark lurking beneath the pier. An insidious danger is already at work, spreading its damage little by little while staying out of sight. Lurking threats are still waiting; insidious ones are doing their harm right now.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

harmless: causing no damage at all

overt: done or shown openly, without concealment

Where it sits · how much hidden harm it carries — creeping → insidious → treacherous

creeping vs. insidious: Creeping notes only the slow, quiet advance -- a creeping vine climbs the wall harmlessly enough -- while insidious adds real damage waiting at the end of that quiet approach.

treacherous vs. insidious: Treacherous raises the stakes past insidious: an insidious danger does its harm before you spot it, while a treacherous one betrays you outright, striking from the very place you trusted most.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: in, on, upon (not the negating in-) (Latin in-)

Root — sid

Root — sid: to sit (from Latin sedere, 'to sit'; insidiae meant 'an ambush')

Suffix — -ious

Suffix — -ious: full of; possessing the qualities of (Latin -osus, via Old French -ous)

Put it together

Put it together: Insidious uses the -ious variant of this unit's suffix family. In- ('in, on, upon' — not the negating in- you may remember from earlier morpheme study) + sid ('to sit,' from Latin sedere) + -ious ('full of'): Latin insidiae meant 'an ambush' — from insidere, 'to sit in or upon,' because ambushers literally sit in wait. Something insidious is 'full of ambush': it settles in quietly, sits unnoticed, and springs its harm only after it has taken hold.

Use the root in a new word: sediment

Use the root in a new word: sediment: By morning, a layer of sediment had settled at the bottom of the jar of river water.

Word Choice

Insidious is for harm that spreads gradually and stays hidden: an insidious disease, an insidious habit, insidious propaganda. Keep this unit's three 'bad' words in their lanes -- insidious harm creeps in unseen, nefarious schemes are openly wicked and criminal, and egregious errors are shockingly bad in plain view.
